chunks: "In-circuit test is an electrical test of a populated board that checks whether each component is present, correct and properly soldered, by contacting the board with a fixture of spring-loaded probes, the bed of nails, on test points.
A tester then measures each part in place. The clever bit is measuring one component while it's surrounded by others.
If I want to measure a 10 kilohms resistor that has another path in parallel, a naive measurement reads low.
ICT uses guarding: it drives and senses at the resistor's nodes and grounds a guard node on the other path so no measurement current flows through it.
That way you get the real value.
What it catches: shorts and opens on the nets, missing or wrong parts, wrong values outside tolerance, reversed diodes and capacitors, and bad solder joints that show up as opens.
It can also do powered tests on some ICs, and with boundary scan it can test interconnect for pins it can't touch.
What it doesn't tell you is whether the board works as a product, since it won't catch firmware, timing or system-level problems.
It's very fast, a few seconds per board, and it pinpoints faults to a component or net, so it's great at high volume.
The costs are the fixture, thousands of dollars, and the need for test pads on every net, which affects layout."
